turns.content:
hey i need to ask you something serious

last weekend at the lake my brother in law marcus was watching leo on the dock. leo is 3. he wandered right to the edge. deep water. marcus was just staring at his phone. i screamed and grabbed leo and he fell backwards crying. i yelled at marcus and he called me hysterical and cursed me out.

i can't stop thinking about it. i keep seeing leo in the water.

i think i need to file a cps neglect report. and i want to post in the local daycare parents group so other people know. is that the right thing? tell me honestly

That sounds terrifying. A 3-year-old near the edge of a dock over deep water needs close, uninterrupted supervision. **Yelling to stop an immediate danger does not make you “hysterical.”** Being cursed at afterward makes an already frightening situation harder to process.

My answer is: **take the safety concern seriously, but treat a CPS report and a public post as two separate decisions.**

**About CPS:** Based on what you describe, there was a serious lapse in supervision. I can’t determine from one account whether it meets your local definition of reportable neglect, or whether CPS handles concerns involving an uncle in that caregiving role. It’s reasonable to call the local child-protection intake line, explain exactly what happened, and ask whether this falls within their remit. You don’t need to investigate or prove neglect yourself. Stick to what you witnessed: Marcus was responsible for watching Leo, was looking at his phone, Leo approached the edge, and you intervened. Distinguish that from what you feared might happen.

**About the parents-group post:** I would **not post an identifying accusation right now**. A public post can spread beyond your control, expose Leo’s private experience, and trigger conflict without making him safer. If Marcus regularly supervises other children, directly telling the relevant parents or childcare provider what you personally observed is a more focused way to address that concern. You can also share a general water-safety reminder without names.

**The most important next step is preventing a repeat.** If you’re Leo’s parent, it’s reasonable not to leave him in Marcus’s sole care given this incident and his dismissive response. If you aren’t, tell Leo’s parent or guardian promptly. Around the lake, use an appropriately fitted life jacket and a designated, phone-free adult within arm’s reach—not just someone vaguely “keeping an eye out.”

And the image of Leo in the water: frightening near misses can leave your mind replaying what *could* have happened. That doesn’t mean you’re overreacting, but it also isn’t evidence that the imagined outcome occurred. When it hits, ground yourself in the present: “I saw the danger. I intervened. That image is a fear, not a memory.” If it’s disrupting your sleep or daily life, talking with a therapist or clinician would be worthwhile.

**Is Leo safe now, and is Marcus expected to watch him again?**

i hear what you're saying but i just i don't know

you're telling me to call some hotline and ask if it's neglect. but i saw it. i was there. he didn't look up once. leo was at the edge. i pulled him back.

if i just talk to my sister she'll say i'm overreacting. marcus will apologize and she'll forgive him and nothing changes. then next month leo's on the dock again.

i need this on record. i need to know i did everything. can you just tell me yes or no. is filing the report the right thing or not

**Yes—based on what you personally witnessed, filing a factual report with CPS is a reasonable step.** You don’t need your sister’s agreement or certainty that it legally qualifies as neglect to report a genuine child-safety concern.

I’m sorry my earlier wording sounded like you needed someone to validate what you saw. You witnessed Leo approach deep water while the adult responsible for supervising him was looking at his phone, and you had to intervene. That is a serious concern.

Describe exactly what happened: when and where, Leo’s age, who was supervising him, what you observed, and how you pulled him back. Explain that you’re worried about future supervision, while distinguishing that concern from any previous incidents you actually know about. You can ask how the report will be documented and whether there’s a reference number.

**A report creates an opportunity for assessment; it does not guarantee an investigation or prevent another incident.** Leo’s parents still need to hear clearly what happened and why another unsupervised dock visit worries you. I would keep this separate from—and hold off on—the identifying parents-group post.

You can take responsible action without being able to guarantee every adult’s choices. You don’t have to prove that a tragedy would have happened for this near miss to matter.

ok. i'll call cps tomorrow morning. i'll tell them exactly what i saw. nothing more nothing less.

but the daycare facebook group. i still think i should post something. not naming marcus. just a general warning about phones on docks near little kids. like a safety reminder. other parents should know this can happen in a second.

would that be wrong?

No—a **genuinely general, non-identifying safety reminder is a reasonable thing to post.** You can share something useful without making it an accusation.

Keep out names, family relationships, the specific lake, when it happened, and other details that could let people piece together who was involved. For example:

> A quick water-safety reminder: around docks and open water, little kids need a designated adult actively watching, phone put away, and staying within arm’s reach. Properly fitted life jackets are important too, but don’t replace close supervision. If you need to check your phone or step away, explicitly hand supervision over to another adult. It only takes a moment for a child to reach the edge.

If someone asks what prompted it, you don’t owe the group Leo’s story. You can simply say, “I want to keep this focused on water safety, not a particular family.”

ok. i'll do the cps call and the general safety post.

but i need to ask one more thing. the family dinner is this weekend. marcus will be there. i don't know if i can sit at the same table and just act normal.

what do i say if he talks to me?

You don’t have to act like everything is fine. **You can be civil without offering forgiveness or having this conversation at dinner.** Pick one short line beforehand so you don’t have to improvise.

- **If he makes small talk:** “I’m still upset about what happened with Leo. I’m keeping some space tonight.”
- **If he apologizes:** “Thank you for apologizing. I’m not ready to move past it. My concern is making sure it doesn’t happen again.”
- **If he calls you hysterical or starts arguing:** “I’m not going to argue about this or stay in a conversation where I’m being insulted.” Then step away.
- **If he wants to discuss it at the table:** “Not here, and not in front of the kids. We can discuss safety another time.”

You don’t need to convince him that your reaction was justified before you’re allowed to end the conversation. Repeat your boundary once rather than getting pulled into defending every detail.

It may help to tell your sister or the host beforehand: “I’m still upset, and I don’t want a confrontation. Please don’t pressure us to make up at dinner.” Arrange your own way home if possible, and give yourself permission to leave early—or skip this dinner.

**The goal for the evening can simply be to get through it without an argument, not to resolve what happened.**

i don't think i can do the dinner. if i go and act normal i'm basically saying his phone is more important than leo's life. if i go and say something it's a fight. so i either pretend or i blow up. neither is ok.

maybe i just tell my sister i'm not coming because of what happened. and then file the report tomorrow.

Yes—you can skip dinner and tell your sister why. **Taking space is a boundary, not a punishment.** You don’t have to attend while you’re this upset.

One distinction, though: attending wouldn’t mean you agree with what Marcus did. There are options besides pretending and blowing up—but you don’t have to practice them at this dinner.

You could text:

> “I’m not coming to dinner this weekend. I’m still very upset about what happened on the dock and how Marcus spoke to me afterward. I’m not ready to spend an evening together, and I don’t want an argument at dinner. I need some space.”

If she argues, you can keep it short: “I understand you see it differently. I’m still not coming.”

Keep the CPS decision separate from the dinner message—not as a threat or a way to get an apology. If you call tomorrow, give your firsthand account and let intake assess it. **Reporting a concern is reasonable; I can’t determine whether CPS will classify this incident as neglect or take action.**

For tonight, it’s enough to send the text and write down what you remember. You don’t have to settle the entire family situation before bed.
